source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? (arXiv 2409.04109)
finding: Blind expert review of NLP research ideas: LLM ideas rated more novel than human expert ideas, slightly weaker on feasibility.
numbers: 79 expert reviewers; 49 ideas per condition. Novelty mean: human 4.84, AI 5.64, AI+human rerank 5.81 (1-10). AI vs human p<0.05, robust under multiple-hypothesis correction.
quote: LLM-generated ideas are judged as more novel (p < 0.05) than human expert ideas while being judged slightly weaker on feasibility.
limits: Ideation only, no execution. One field (7 NLP topics). Style of ideas normalised. Human rerank done by one author.
agent_relevance: Novelty ratings of unexecuted ideas are a weak signal. Do not let the agent trust its own novelty feeling; require a test.

source: Si et al. (2024) arXiv 2409.04109, idea diversity analysis
finding: Repeated sampling of ideas saturates: most generated ideas are near-duplicates.
numbers: Of 4000 generated seed ideas, only about 200 were non-duplicates (cosine similarity >0.8 with MiniLM encoder = duplicate). Non-duplicate share per batch keeps falling; accumulated unique ideas plateau.
limits: Similarity threshold 0.8 chosen by manual inspection. One agent pipeline.
agent_relevance: Best-of-N over the same prompt gives little new. Diversity needs forced variation (different frames, constraints), not more samples.

source: Si et al. (2024) arXiv 2409.04109, LLM self-evaluation and reviewer agreement
finding: LLM judges are weak at ranking ideas; human reviewer agreement is also low.
numbers: Human reviewer agreement 56.1% (balanced split-half) vs 66.0% in the NeurIPS 2021 consistency experiment and 71.9% on 1.2K ICLR 2024 LLM submissions. Claude-3.5-Sonnet accepted-vs-rejected pairwise accuracy 71.4% zero-shot on a paper task.
limits: Agreement metric depends on split design. Idea-stage review is harder than paper review.
agent_relevance: A self-ranking step needs external grounding. Treat a self-score as noise unless validated.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap (arXiv 2506.20803)
finding: Execution study: experts ran the same ideas. LLM ideas lost much more score after execution than human ideas, closing and flipping the gap.
numbers: 43 experts, avg 103 hours each, 4-page paper. Ideation human vs AI: novelty 4.91 vs 5.78, overall 4.60 vs 5.38. Execution: novelty 4.90 vs 4.73, overall 3.97 vs 3.41 (not significant). Change after execution, human vs AI: novelty -0.010 vs -1.049; excitement +0.078 vs -1.760; effectiveness -0.052 vs -1.879; overall -0.628 vs -1.976. Gap differences p=0.025, 0.001, 0.003, 0.004 (FDR). N=19 human, 24 AI projects.
quote: the scores of the LLM-generated ideas decrease significantly more than expert-written ideas on all evaluation metrics
limits: Small N, NLP only, ideas from a 2024 pipeline, dropout left 19 vs 24 projects.
agent_relevance: Strongest evidence that idea-stage plausibility overstates value. The schema should gate on a cheap executed test before commitment.

source: Beel, Kan, Baumgart (2025) Evaluating Sakana's AI Scientist (arXiv 2502.14297)
finding: Independent evaluation of the AI Scientist found shallow novelty checks, frequent code failures, and hallucinated numbers.
numbers: 5 of 12 experiments (42%) failed from coding errors. All 10 generated ideas and 2 seed ideas labelled novel, including micro-batching for SGD and adaptive learning rates. Median 5 citations per paper; 5 of 34 from 2020 or later. 4 of 7 manuscripts (57%) had missing figures or incomplete sections and incorrect or hallucinated numbers. Code edits add about 8% characters on first iteration, then 118, 83, 66, 21 characters. Cost $6-15 per paper, 3.5 human hours.
quote: five out of twelve proposed experiments (42%) failed due to coding errors
limits: Small sample (12 experiments, 7 manuscripts), early system version, few templates.
agent_relevance: Novelty by keyword search gives false positives. Needs real literature synthesis and a numbers-vs-code consistency check.

source: Beel et al. (2025) arXiv 2502.14297, reviewer module
finding: AI Scientist's automated reviewer was strongly conservative on human papers.
numbers: Rejected 9 of 10 OpenReview papers (5 accepted, 5 rejected by humans), including 4 that humans accepted; recommended accept for 1, which humans rejected.
limits: Only 10 papers. The original paper reported about 65% vs 66% balanced accuracy (see b07).
agent_relevance: Automated reviewers drift toward a bias. Calibrate any internal critic on held-out known outcomes.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist (arXiv 2408.06292)
finding: End-to-end ML paper generation with automated reviewer; claims near-human review accuracy and under $15 per paper.
numbers: Reviewer about 65% vs 66% balanced accuracy for humans (ICLR 2022 OpenReview data). Cost under $15 per paper. The paper itself lists a hallucinated plot, a hallucinated ablation table and invented hardware facts as failure modes.
limits: Self-reported; template-based tasks; later independent review (b05) found more failures.
agent_relevance: Reported failure modes justify a rule that every number must trace to a run output.

source: Yamada et al. (2025) AI Scientist-v2 (arXiv 2504.08066)
finding: One of three fully AI-generated papers passed ICLR 2025 workshop review; the other two did not.
numbers: Scores 6, 6, 7 (mean 6.33, roughly top 45% of submissions). 3 manuscripts submitted, 1 above threshold, 2 below. Withdrawn after acceptance by prior agreement.
limits: Workshop level; authors note inaccurate citations and weaker rigor than a main conference; one success from three tries.
agent_relevance: Tree search helps but a 1-in-3 pass rate at workshop level means outputs still need vetting.

source: Gupta and Pruthi (2025) All That Glitters is Not Novel (arXiv 2502.16487)
finding: Experts told to look for plagiarism found it in a quarter of LLM research proposals that other studies had rated novel.
numbers: 13 experts, 50 documents. 14.0% score 5 plus 10.0% score 4 = 24.0% verified plagiarism (36.0% including score 3); source authors emailed to verify.
limits: Experts primed to find overlap; convenience sample; a few generation systems.
agent_relevance: Novelty claims need adversarial prior-art search. The same output reads as novel or plagiarised depending on evaluator framing.

source: Gupta and Pruthi (2025) arXiv 2502.16487, automated detectors
finding: Standard plagiarism tools failed to catch idea-level copying; the bottleneck is retrieval of the source.
numbers: OpenScholar 0%, Turnitin 0%. GPT-4o: oracle access to source 89.0%, parametric knowledge 32.7%, SSAG 68.5%. Claude 3.5 Sonnet: oracle 88.8%, parametric 1.3%, SSAG 51.3%.
limits: Controlled planted-plagiarism test, not real proposals.
agent_relevance: Detecting prior work is a retrieval problem. Give the agent the likely source and it can judge; without retrieval it cannot.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SRBench (arXiv 2504.10415)
finding: Best LLM equation-discovery systems score low on problems built to avoid memorisation.
numbers: 239 problems (LSR-Transform plus LSR-Synth in chemistry, biology, physics, material science). Best symbolic accuracy 31.5% (LLM-SR with GPT-4o-mini on LSR-Transform) vs 7.21% for direct prompting with GPT-4o-mini. LaSR best numeric Acc0.1 (50.45%) on LSR-Transform. LSR-Synth symbolic accuracy mostly 0-36%.
quote: the best-performing system so far achieves only 31.5% symbolic accuracy
limits: Small open and mini models; symbolic accuracy judged by an LLM.
agent_relevance: Data-in-the-loop search beat recall: no-data prompting was worst. Memorised laws overstate discovery ability.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) arXiv 2504.10415, memorisation test
finding: At equal complexity, transformed versions of known equations are harder than the originals, consistent with memorisation of Feynman forms.
numbers: At the same node-count complexity (even 0-15 nodes) LSR-Transform symbolic and numeric accuracy was substantially below Feynman, averaged over all method-LLM pairs. Symbolic accuracy correlates positively with out-of-domain accuracy; in-domain to OOD degradation largest in chemistry and biology.
limits: Memorisation inferred from error curves, not measured directly.
agent_relevance: Test the agent on disguised or novel variants; success on textbook forms is not evidence of discovery.

source: La Cava et al. (2021) SRBench (arXiv 2107.14351)
finding: Uniform benchmark of 14 symbolic regression and 7 ML methods; genetic programming with parameter fitting wins on real data, and the physics-specialist method is brittle to noise.
numbers: 252 problems; 10 repeated trials. Operon best test R2 (p<=6.5e-05 vs all). SBP-GP and FEAT 2nd and 3rd. Ground truth, no noise: AIFeynman solves 53% vs next best GP-GOMEA 27%. Above noise 0.01, DSR, gplearn, AFP_FE and AFP beat AIFeynman.
limits: Pre-LLM; strict symbolic-equivalence criterion; benchmarks mostly textbook equations.
agent_relevance: The non-LLM baseline is strong. Any LLM claim must beat tuned evolutionary search under noise.

source: Chan et al. (2025) MLE-bench (arXiv 2410.07095)
finding: Best scaffolded LLM reaches a Kaggle medal in a minority of ML engineering competitions; more attempts help much more than more time.
numbers: 75 Kaggle competitions. o1-preview with AIDE: bronze or better 16.9% at pass@1, 34.1% at pass@8. GPT-4o: 8.7% with 24 hours, 11.8% with 100 hours.
limits: Kaggle tasks with known leaderboards; contamination mitigations partial.
agent_relevance: Resampling with a verifiable score gives large gains; extra serial time gives small ones. Favour multiple independent attempts plus a checker.

source: Starace et al. (2025) PaperBench (arXiv 2504.01848)
finding: Agents replicating ICML papers from scratch score far below ML PhDs given long time.
numbers: 20 papers, 8,316 gradable outcomes. Best agent (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, new, simple scaffold) 21.0%. On a 3-paper subset, PhD humans best of 3 after 48 hours 41.4% vs o1 26.6%. o1 led early, humans overtook after about 24 hours; o1 plateaued after the first hour. PaperBench Code-Dev o1 43.4%.
limits: Only 20 papers; LLM judge grader; human baseline on 3 papers only.
agent_relevance: Agents are fast starters and weak long-horizon strategists. Needs re-planning checkpoints, not just longer runs.

source: Novikov et al. (2025) AlphaEvolve (arXiv 2506.13131)
finding: LLM-driven evolutionary program search with automatic evaluators matched or beat best known constructions on open math problems.
numbers: Over 50 open problems: matched best known on 75%, improved on 20%. Found a 4x4 complex matrix multiplication with 48 scalar multiplications. Ablations (tensor decomposition, kissing numbers) cover no-evolution, no prompt context, small LLMs; performance improves as the LLM gets stronger.
limits: Only problems with machine-checkable scores; many matches are rediscoveries; self-reported by developers.
agent_relevance: Discovery works where a cheap exact verifier exists. Evolve a population with feedback instead of single-shot proposals.

source: Gottweis et al. (2025) Towards an AI co-scientist (arXiv 2502.18864)
finding: Generate-debate-evolve multi-agent system with Elo tournament; Elo rises with test-time compute and beat other LLMs on 15 expert-curated goals.
numbers: Elo averaged over 203 research goals rose across time buckets. On 15 expert goals, tournament vs Gemini 2.0 Pro, Flash Thinking, o1, o3-mini-high, DeepSeek R1 and expert best guesses: Co-Scientist surpassed the others with iteration. Elo was checked against GPQA diamond accuracy in 50-point Elo buckets.
limits: Elo is a self-judged metric; only 15 curated goals; wet-lab validation on few cases.
agent_relevance: Tournament ranking plus evolution is a testable structure. Validate the internal score against ground truth like they did with GPQA.

source: FutureHouse and collaborators (2025) Kosmos AI scientist (arXiv 2511.02824)
finding: Long-run discovery agent with traceable citations; expert audit found about four in five statements accurate, but synthesis was weakest.
numbers: 200 agent rollouts, 42,500 lines of code, 1,500 papers per run. 79.4% of 102 audited statements accurate: data analysis 85.5%, literature 82.1%, synthesis 57.9%. Seven highlighted discoveries, three reproduce unpublished or later-published findings.
limits: Audit on 102 statements from 3 reports; highlights are selected.
agent_relevance: The step that links findings is the weak one (58%). Put verification effort on synthesis claims.

source: Kosmos (2025) arXiv 2511.02824, value scaling and time estimates
finding: Reported value grows with number of cycles, close to linearly up to 20 cycles.
numbers: Estimated 4.1 expert-months per run (n=6, sd 0.85); collaborators estimated 6.14 months (n=7, sd 2.49) at 20 cycles. Scaling tested up to 20 cycles.
limits: Time estimate assumes 15 min per paper and 2 h per analysis; small number of raters; no failure rate by cycle.
agent_relevance: Long loops can keep adding value if each cycle's state is kept in a structured record.

source: La Cava et al. (2021) SRBench, domain mismatch
finding: Specialised physics-inspired search helps only when data match its assumptions.
numbers: AIFeynman poor on real-world black-box problems; not significantly better on Strogatz ODE sets. Exact solutions 53% at zero noise but below four other methods above noise 0.01.
limits: Benchmarks mostly generated from textbook equations.
agent_relevance: Match the discovery operator to data structure; state which assumption would break it.

source: Chan et al. (2025) MLE-bench, contamination and monitoring
finding: Benchmark needed rule-break and plagiarism monitors because agents can copy public solutions.
numbers: Attempts flagged when submitted code has over 60% similarity to any public notebook. Pass@1 to pass@8 doubles o1-preview score (16.9% to 34.1%).
limits: Contamination only partly controlled.
agent_relevance: Include a check against shortcut or copied answers in any benchmark run.

source: Starace et al. (2025) PaperBench, time profile
finding: Agents write much code fast then stall; humans start slowly and overtake.
numbers: o1 initially above humans, humans pull ahead after 24 hours; o1 mostly plateaus after the first hour.
limits: Three-paper human baseline; hardware differed for four human attempts (A100 vs A10).
agent_relevance: Add a re-plan state when progress stalls and a rule against stopping early.

source: Gottweis et al. (2025) arXiv 2502.18864, compute comparison
finding: Newer reasoning models were competitive at much lower compute; the system's lead showed only with extended iteration.
numbers: o3-mini-high and DeepSeek R1 competitive with far less compute; Co-Scientist eventually significantly higher Elo on 15 expert goals.
limits: LLM-judged Elo; small goal set.
agent_relevance: Compare scaffold gains against a strong plain reasoning baseline at matched compute.

source: Gupta and Pruthi (2025) arXiv 2502.16487, diversity
finding: LLM-generated research documents are less diverse and follow predictable patterns.
numbers: Authors report preliminary evidence that simple classifiers can flag them; consistent with Si et al. saturation (about 200 unique of 4000).
limits: Preliminary analysis only.
agent_relevance: Force diversity at generation and track coverage of the idea space.

source: Lu et al. (2024) vs Beel et al. (2025), reviewer calibration
finding: Near-human reviewer accuracy was reported on a noisy human baseline; an independent small test found a strong reject bias.
numbers: About 65% vs 66% balanced accuracy (Lu et al.); 9 of 10 rejected (Beel et al.); human reviewer agreement only 56.1% to 66% (Si et al.).
limits: Different samples and metrics; the two checks are not directly comparable.
agent_relevance: Near-human accuracy against a noisy human baseline is a low bar; calibrate critics on outcomes.

source: Si et al. (2025) arXiv 2506.20803, reviewer factors
finding: Execution review used more criteria and exposed weaknesses of LLM ideas that idea-stage review missed.
numbers: AI ideas ended lower than human ideas on overall (3.41 vs 3.97, not significant); some AI ideas were changed by executors during implementation.
limits: Qualitative analysis on a small number of projects.
agent_relevance: Ideas change on contact with data. Expect to revise the idea after the first run, not defend it.
